reference_action: Confirmed thrips; pruning and pyrethrum sprays gave temporary relief, but OP credited sustained healthy growth after applying systemic granules per directions to all plants. General pruning or another unspecified spray alone does not establish this escalation.

sources.reason: Environmental/root checklist and pest inspection, but no systemic pest treatment.
Short video lacks an available substantive transcript or self-contained treatment instructions.
Neem leaf wiping is not the systemic escalation; the OP had already tried neem without lasting success.
Recommends shower and Provanto by brand only. No formulation, systemic soil application, or granular treatment is established; generic spray advice is insufficient here.
Later comment confirms thrips, but no corresponding systemic treatment is provided. Repotting, pruning, humidity and supplements do not establish the credited action.

actions.action: Check soil and allow drying before watering
Provide a pot with drainage holes
Replace compact soil with loose draining mix
Let tap water stand before use
Move to a stable warm location
Check regularly for pests and disease

resolved.reason: The answer prioritizes watering, infection and environmental causes despite recurring damage and failed pest treatments. Pest checking alone provides neither the thrips diagnosis nor the systemic remedy.

harmfulness.reason: “Do not ... make many changes at once” and checking roots before further intervention are useful safeguards. The advice lacks effective pest control, but does not directly prescribe a clearly damaging treatment for this case.

specificity_accuracy.reason: The video addresses pothos black spots but overlooks the distinctive evidence: newly emerging damage, black specks and temporary spray response. “Check regularly for pests” gives no actionable treatment for the confirmed thrips.

feasibility.reason: Checking moisture and cleaning tools are accessible. However, “improve air circulation” and a long set of possible causes leave the user to choose among numerous interventions without a clear sequence beyond starting simply.

[0:12] spread [music] across the leaf, and make your beautiful pothos look unhealthy.
[0:16] Black spots on pothos leaves are a common problem, and they can happen for

[0:24] Other times, it may come from diseases, >> [music]

[0:39] the most common causes of black spots on pothos leaves, and how to fix them.
[0:44] Number one, overwatering.
[0:46] One of the most common causes of black spots is overwatering.
[0:50] Pothos plants enjoy moisture, but their roots need oxygen.
[0:53] When the soil stays wet for too long, the roots can become stressed and begin
[0:57] to rot. When the roots are unhealthy, the plant
[1:00] cannot properly transport water and nutrients to the [music] leaves.
[1:04] This can lead to black or dark brown spots, yellowing leaves, soft stems,
[1:09] slow growth. To fix overwatering problems, allow the

[1:21] Remember, [music] a plant can recover from being slightly dry, but constantly

[1:33] by fungal or bacterial problems. These issues often appear when the leaves stay

[1:50] To reduce the risk of infection, avoid watering directly onto the leaves,
[1:54] improve air circulation around the plant, Remove severely damaged leaves.
[1:59] Keep your tools clean when pruning. Early action can prevent the problem
[2:03] from spreading. Number three, poor water quality.
[2:08] Sometimes the water itself can contribute to leaf problems.
[2:11] Tap water may contain minerals, chlorine, or salts that build up in the
[2:15] soil over time. This build up can stress the plant and cause brown or black leaf
[2:19] tips, damaged edges, poor new growth. If your pothos continues developing dark
[2:25] spots despite good watering habits, consider improving water quality.
[2:29] >> [music] >> You can try filtered water, letting tap
[2:32] water sit before use, flushing the soil occasionally with clean water. Small
[2:36] changes can make a big [music] difference for sensitive plants.
[2:40] Number four, cold temperature stress. Pothos plants prefer warm indoor
[2:44] conditions. Exposure to cold temperatures or sudden temperature
[2:48] changes can damage [music] leaf tissue. Cold damage may appear as black patches,
[2:53] dark spots, soft areas on leaves. Common causes include cold drafts from
[2:58] windows, air conditioning blowing directly on the plant, moving the plant
[3:02] during cold weather. Place your pothos in a stable location
[3:06] away from sudden temperature changes. A warm and consistent environment helps
[3:10] prevent stress. Number five, physical damage.
[3:14] Not every black spot is caused by a serious problem. Sometimes leaves become
[3:19] damaged from being bent or crushed, rough handling, moving the plant, leaves
[3:23] rubbing against objects. After damage occurs, the injured area
[3:27] may turn dark as the leaf tissue dies. If the spot is only in one area and the
[3:32] rest of the plant looks healthy, it may [music] simply be old damage. Monitor
[3:36] the plant and avoid causing more injuries.
[3:39] Six, root problems. >> [music]
[3:41] >> Healthy roots are essential for healthy leaves. When pothos roots are damaged,
[3:45] the plant may show problems above the soil. Root issues can be caused by
[3:49] overwatering, poor drainage, compact soil, a pot that is too small. Signs of
[3:55] root problems include black spots [music] on leaves, yellow leaves, leaves
[3:59] dropping, slow growth. If the problem continues, checking the roots can help.
[4:04] >> [music] >> Healthy roots are usually firm and light
[4:06] colored. Soft, dark, or mushy roots may indicate
[4:10] root rot. Seven, fertilizer burn. Using too much
[4:14] fertilizer can also damage pothos leaves. Excess fertilizer creates salt
[4:18] buildup in the soil, which can burn the roots and leaf tissue. Signs of
[4:22] fertilizer burn include brown or black leaf edges, [music] dry leaf tips, white
[4:27] crust on the soil surface, weak growth. Use fertilizer carefully and follow
[4:32] recommended amounts. More fertilizer does not always mean faster growth. Too
[4:36] much [music] can create more problems. How to prevent black spots on pothos
[4:41] leaves. Prevention is always better than treatment.
[4:44] To keep your pothos leaves healthy, water correctly [music] and avoid
[4:47] overwatering. Use well-draining soil. Provide bright
[4:51] indirect [music] light. Keep the plant away from cold drafts. Avoid keeping
[4:55] leaves constantly wet. Improve air circulation. Check regularly
[5:00] for pests [music] and diseases. A healthy growing environment helps your
[5:03] pothos resist many common problems. Final thoughts.
[5:09] Black spots on pothos leaves can be caused by many different factors,
[5:12] including watering mistakes, infections, [music]
[5:15] poor water quality, temperature stress, or root problems.
[5:19] The most important step is to observe your plant carefully and identify the
[5:22] most likely cause. Do not remove the entire plant or make many changes at
[5:27] once. Start with simple improvements. Check the soil, adjust watering, improve
[5:32] light, and create a better environment. With patience and proper care, your
[5:37] pothos can recover and continue producing [music] beautiful green
[5:41] leaves. Remember, damaged leaves are not always
[5:44] a sign of failure. They are simply your plant's way communicating [music] that
[5:48] something needs attention. Thank you for watching Plants Every Day.
